title: Building a budget with a cost breakdown structure
blurb: Turn work package estimates into a time-phased budget using a CBS, then add contingency and management reserve in the right places.
question: A city council is refurbishing its central library. The project manager has an approved WBS and an estimate for every work package. The sponsor asks how these will become a budget the board can approve and then control spending against. What should the project manager do, and what should the budget contain?

teach.h: A budget is the plan for money
teach.body: Formally, the project budget is the agreed, time-phased amount of money needed to deliver the scope, built up from the cost estimates and approved as the baseline against which spending is controlled. In plain English: what will it cost, what is each pound for, and when will we spend it? Without that, nobody can tell whether the project is on track financially, or fund it at the right time.

teach.h: WBS says what, CBS says how much
teach.body: The cost breakdown structure (CBS) organises every cost into a hierarchy, aligned to the WBS so each work package has its own cost code. Costs can also be grouped by type (labour, materials, equipment, subcontracts, overheads). The benefits: nothing is missed or counted twice, estimates roll up to a total, and actual costs can later be booked to the same codes, so the PM can see exactly where money is going.

teach.caption: Each box is a cost code. Project management and other costs would sit in the CBS too; the tree is simplified.
Spending starts slowly (design, mobilising), climbs steeply in the busy middle, then tails off during handover. The finance team uses this cash-flow profile to make the money available on time.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Start from the scope: list every work package and the resources it needs (from the WBS).
Estimate each one and organise the costs in a CBS aligned to the WBS, so nothing is missed or double counted.
Time-phase the costs against the schedule to show when money is needed (cash-flow profile/S-curve).
Add contingency for identified risks; note any management reserve held by the sponsor for unknowns.
Get the budget approved and baselined so actual costs can be monitored against it.
Budget = estimates rolled up through a CBS, time-phased, plus contingency, then approved as a baseline.
The CBS mirrors the WBS: each work package gets a cost code, so actuals can be tracked.
Cumulative planned spend usually forms an S-curve.
Contingency: identified risks, inside the baseline. Management reserve: unknowns, held by the sponsor/board.
Linear: whole-project bottom-up budget released at gates. Iterative: fixed cost per time box, scope flexes.

summary: You can now explain how a budget is built from work package estimates through a CBS, time-phased into an S-curve, with contingency and management reserve placed correctly. You can also explain how budgeting differs between linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a cost breakdown structure (CBS) when building a project budget?
options: To show who is accountable for each task
To organise every cost against the work
To rank risks by probability and impact
To show the order in which work happens
A.why: A CBS organises all the project's costs into a structure aligned to the WBS, so nothing is missed or double counted and actuals can be tracked to each work package.

whyNot.0: Accountability for work packages is shown by the OBS combined with the WBS in a RACI chart, not the CBS.
whyNot.2: Ranking risks is done with a probability and impact grid in risk analysis.
whyNot.3: Sequence is shown in a network diagram or Gantt chart, not the CBS.

A.q: A project manager spreads each work package's cost across the months in which the work is scheduled. What is this called?
options: Resource levelling the budget
Re-estimating the WBS
Baselining the risk register
Time-phasing the budget
A.why: Time-phasing links costs to the schedule, showing when money will be needed. Plotted cumulatively it usually gives an S-curve.

whyNot.0: Resource levelling delays activities to stay within resource limits; it is a scheduling technique.
whyNot.1: Re-estimating refines estimates as information improves; it doesn't spread costs across months.
whyNot.2: The risk register is not baselined in this way, and this activity is about cost over time.

A.q: Which statement best describes project contingency?
options: Money set aside for identified risks
Money held by the board for unknowns
Money used to fund approved new scope
Money kept to reward the team at the end
A.why: Contingency is a provision of money (and time) for identified risks that may occur, sized from risk analysis and drawn down through an agreed process.

whyNot.1: Money held by the sponsor or board for unknowns is management reserve.
whyNot.2: Approved new scope is funded through change control, which adjusts the baseline.
whyNot.3: Contingency is never a reward pot; unused contingency is released back to the organisation.

B.q: During budgeting, a team finds the same scaffolding hire appears in two different work packages. What should they do?
options: Keep both entries as a safety margin
Move both entries into contingency
Assign it to one cost code in the CBS
Ask the sponsor to raise the budget
B.why: A well-structured CBS gives each cost one home, so the budget is neither inflated by double counting nor missing items.

whyNot.0: Double counting hides real costs and inflates the budget; safety margins belong in contingency, sized from risk.
whyNot.1: Contingency is for identified risks, not a place to park duplicated estimates.
whyNot.3: The fix is to correct the structure, not to increase the budget.

B.q: Why does the cumulative planned spend of a typical project form an S-curve?
options: Spend is slow early, fast in the middle, slow at the end
Spend is high early, then falls steadily to the end
Spend is the same every month across the whole project
Spend rises only when contingency is drawn down
B.why: Early work (design, mobilisation) costs little, the busy delivery middle costs most, and handover tails off, giving a shallow-steep-shallow cumulative curve.

whyNot.1: A high-then-falling spend rate would give a curve that is steep first, not an S.
whyNot.2: Equal monthly spend would give a straight cumulative line, not an S-curve.
whyNot.3: Contingency drawdown is occasional; it doesn't create the S shape of planned spend.

B.q: Who normally holds and controls the management reserve?
options: The project team
The project manager
The sponsor or board
The main supplier
B.why: Management reserve is for unknowns and sits outside the cost baseline, so it is held by the sponsor or board rather than the PM.

whyNot.0: The team works within the budget it is given; it doesn't control reserves.
whyNot.1: The PM manages the cost baseline and contingency within agreed rules, but not the management reserve.
whyNot.3: A supplier manages its own contract price; it never holds the client's reserves.

C.q: An organisation runs an iterative project with a dedicated team of six working in two-week time boxes. How is its budget MOST likely to be built?
options: Team cost per time box times the number planned
A bottom-up estimate of every detailed requirement
A fixed price agreed after all features are known
The sum of all features in the product backlog
C.why: In iterative delivery, time and cost are fixed per time box (largely the cost of a stable team), and scope flexes to fit, so the budget is driven by team run-rate and the number of time boxes.

whyNot.1: Detailed bottom-up estimates of the full scope are typical of linear projects, where requirements are defined up front.
whyNot.2: In iterative projects the features emerge, so they aren't all known in advance.
whyNot.3: The backlog changes as priorities change; cost is fixed and scope flexes, not the other way round.

C.q: Which TWO statements about contingency are correct? 1: It is sized from analysis of identified risks. 2: It is held outside the cost baseline by the board. 3: It is drawn down through an agreed process. 4: It can fund any extra feature a stakeholder asks for.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: Contingency is sized from risk analysis of identified risks, sits inside the cost baseline and is released through an agreed governance process.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 describes management reserve, which is held outside the baseline.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 describes management reserve, and statement 4 is wrong: new features go through change control.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: contingency is not for new scope.

C.q: Halfway through, a stakeholder asks for an extra reading room. The project manager suggests paying for it from contingency because there is plenty left. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as unspent contingency belongs to the PM
Agree, if the cost is under 10% of the budget
Refuse, as contingency can never be spent at all
Raise a change request; it is new scope, not a risk
C.why: A new reading room is a change to scope. It should be assessed through change control, which may adjust the baseline and funding; contingency is reserved for identified risks.

whyNot.0: Contingency is controlled through governance for identified risks; it doesn't belong to the PM to spend freely.
whyNot.1: There is no rule that small additions can bypass change control; any scope change needs proper assessment.
whyNot.2: Contingency is spent when identified risks occur, through the agreed process; it just isn't for new scope.

reteach.title: Budgeting a wedding
reteach.question: Picture planning a wedding: venue, catering, flowers, outfits, photographer. How would you build a budget you could trust, and what would you hold back for things going wrong?

blocks.h: List it, price it, schedule it, protect it
blocks.body: First list everything the wedding needs (that is your WBS). Price each item and group the costs under headings such as venue, food and clothes (your CBS), so you don't forget the cake or pay for the band twice. Then note when each payment falls due: deposits early, the big bills near the day. Finally, keep a sum back for risks you can name, like rain needing a marquee (contingency), while a parent quietly holds a little extra for the truly unexpected (management reserve).

blocks.caption: The extra money a parent holds back 'just in case' sits outside this budget, like management reserve.

blocks.text: If a cousin asks to add a fireworks display, that's a change, not a risk. You decide whether to fund it; you don't quietly spend the rain money on it.

explain.body: A budget can only be as good as the scope behind it. Start by identifying every work package and the resources each needs, then estimate each one. Missing a work package means missing its cost.

test.q: A PM is about to build a bottom-up budget. What must be in place FIRST?
options: A list of all work and resources
A signed final account statement
A completed earned value report
An agreed management reserve
test.why: Bottom-up budgeting starts from the scope: every work package and the resources it needs must be identified before costs can be estimated.

whyNot.1: A final account statement is produced at closure, not at the start.
whyNot.2: Earned value reports need an existing budget baseline to measure against.
whyNot.3: Management reserve is decided after the base estimate, not before it.

explain.h: The CBS gives every cost a home
explain.body: The CBS arranges costs in a hierarchy aligned to the WBS (and can group them by type). Each work package gets a cost code, so estimates roll up to a total and actual costs can later be booked against the same codes.

test.q: Why is the CBS aligned to the WBS?
options: So risks can be scored by impact
So suppliers can set their own prices
So the team can be motivated by goals
So costs can be tracked by work package
test.why: Aligning cost codes to work packages lets estimates roll up and actual costs be tracked against the specific work that caused them.

whyNot.0: Risk scoring uses probability and impact in risk analysis, not the CBS.
whyNot.1: Supplier prices are agreed through procurement; the CBS just records the costs.
whyNot.2: Motivation is a leadership matter, unrelated to cost structures.

explain.body: Spreading each cost over the schedule shows when money is needed. Plotted cumulatively this is usually an S-curve: slow start, steep middle, gentle finish. It becomes the baseline that progress and spend are later compared with.

test.q: What does a time-phased budget mainly help the organisation do?
options: Pick the best project life cycle
Have funds ready when needed
Decide the project's success criteria
Score each stakeholder's interest
test.why: Time-phasing shows when money is needed, so finance can make funds available at the right time and spend can be monitored against the plan.

whyNot.0: The life cycle choice depends on the nature of the project, not cash timing.
whyNot.2: Success criteria are agreed with the sponsor and stakeholders during definition.
whyNot.3: Stakeholder analysis uses tools such as power/interest grids.

explain.body: Contingency covers identified risks, sits inside the cost baseline and is released through governance. Management reserve covers unknowns, sits outside the baseline and is held by the sponsor or board.

test.q: A risk on the register, 'ground conditions worse than surveyed', occurs. Which fund is designed for this?
options: Management reserve
Operating budget
Contingency
Sponsor's bonus pot
test.why: This is an identified risk on the register, so its cost is met from contingency through the agreed drawdown process.

whyNot.0: Management reserve is for unknowns, not risks already on the register.
whyNot.1: The operating budget funds business as usual, not project risks.
whyNot.3: There is no such fund in project budgeting.
